info.name: finflow_v2
info.description:
Finflow backend API. Requests are grouped by bounded context, the same way the codebase is (Identity, Ingestion, Merchant, Financial, Alerts). Import the sibling `finflow_v2.postman_environment.json` alongside this file and select it before sending requests.

Auth flow: run Identity > Auth > Register (or Login) once — its test script reads the response and fills `fetch_token`, `token`, and `user_id` on the active environment automatically. Every authenticated request below sends `Authorization: {{token}}`.

See docs/email-forwarding.md and docs/running.md for the narrative version of this API.

item.name: Verification
item.description:
Proving that an address can be read, before an account is built on it. Both requests are unauthenticated and both are deliberately uninformative: the first answers the same way whether or not the address is registered (and sends mail either way), and the second gives one answer for a wrong code, an expired one and an address with no challenge at all.

Rate limited per address: one message a minute, five an hour, answered with 429 and a `Retry-After` header.

request.description:
Mails a six-digit code, valid 15 minutes. Answers 202 in every case — an address that already has an account gets a different message rather than no message, so this cannot be used to ask who is registered here.

Against a local run (`ENVIRONMENT=local`) no mail is sent at all and the code comes back in `code`, which the test script stores as `verification_code`. Anywhere else that field is `null` and the code is only in the mailbox.

exec: // Only a local run echoes the code; elsewhere it
// is null and has to be read from the mailbox.

request.description: Trades the code for the one-time token `POST /identity/register` spends, valid 30 minutes. Five wrong guesses spend the challenge (429); the right code works once. The test script stores the token as `verification_token`.

Creates an account, assigns it a forwarding address, and returns a usable access token. The last step of three: run **Request verification code** and **Confirm verification code** first — `verification_token` is what the second one fills in, and without it registration answers 403. It is spent here, once: a replay of the same request cannot make a second account.

`name` is optional — an account is identified by its email, and a name can be set later via `PATCH /identity/me`. `allowed_domains`/`allowed_addresses` are optional too — approved senders can be set later via `PATCH /identity/inbox`. The forwarding address itself is always assigned regardless; see Identity > Inbox > Get inbox to read it. On success, the test script fills `fetch_token`/`token`/`user_id` on this environment.

Same response as Register for an existing account. Same error for an unknown email and a wrong password on purpose. On success, the test script fills `fetch_token`/`token`/`user_id` on this environment.

The account the bearer token verifies as: id, email and name. Read from storage, so a name changed through `PATCH /identity/me` shows up here immediately — the token itself keeps the `name` it was issued with until the next login.

Changes the caller's name — the only editable field for now, since the email is the account's identity. Whose account is edited comes from the token, so there is no id to pass. Returns the updated account, the same shape as `GET /identity/me`.
The caller's forwarding address (assigned automatically at registration) and who is currently approved to send to it.

Replaces — not merges — who may send to the caller's forwarding address. Leave both lists empty and the address is approved for nobody, the safe default. See docs/email-forwarding.md for the full flow, including how the user then sets up the actual forwarding rule in their own mail client.

item.name: Password
item.description: Recovering a password through the mail, and changing one while logged in. Every one of these ends the sessions opened with the old password — including, for **Change password**, the token that asked, which is why it returns a replacement.

request.description:
Mails a link with a one-time token, valid 30 minutes. Answers 202 and an empty body whether or not the address has an account, and mails something either way — an address with no account gets a message saying so, rather than silence.

Rate limited per address: one a minute, five an hour (429 with `Retry-After`). Asking again retires the previous link.

The token is only in the mail; against a local run it is written to the API's log instead.

Spends the token out of the emailed link and sets the password behind it. 204 and no token: log in with the new password, which is also the proof it worked. Unknown, expired and already-spent links are one answer (400), so this never confirms that a token was real.

Set `password_reset_token` by hand from the link — nothing can fill it automatically, which is the point of it.

For somebody who can still log in. The current password is required even though the request is authenticated: a session left open on a shared machine must not be enough to take the account over. Getting it wrong answers 403, not 401: the token is fine and the session is not over, so a client that reads 401 as "you have been signed out" never sees one here.

Returns a fresh access token because the change invalidates the one that made this request, along with every other session. The test script replaces `fetch_token`/`token` with it.

exec: // The old token stopped working the moment this
// answered: every session is cut, this one too.

request.description: Processing statuses, the reasons behind them, and instrument_kinds — the words a bank alert arrives with. An account declared with any other spelling is accepted and then never matches an alert.

query.description: received | queued | processing | processed | pending_fallback | failed | ignored
true also returns `counts` and `total`. Off by default: the page is read as a page, while the counts read everything the account ever received.

request.description: What arrived for the authenticated caller, newest first — the only read surface ingestion has, and the one that tells the three failures apart: nothing arrived, it arrived from a sender nobody approved (status `ignored`, and its sender is shown so it can be approved), or it arrived and nothing could be read out of it (`pending_fallback`, with `deferred_reason` saying whether a model declined it or none was configured). Never returns the email body. `has_more` says whether another page is behind this one; `counts` and `total` are null unless `with_counts=true` asks for them, and then `counts` is every status this user has, filter or no filter, so a summary line does not move when the list is narrowed. The index behind it is eventually consistent: a message received a moment ago can take an instant to appear.

How far the authenticated caller got connecting their bank, for the screen that walks them through it. Four steps — `address_assigned`, `senders_approved`, `forwarding_confirmed`, `first_alert` — each with `done` and, for the two that are events rather than states, `at` (epoch seconds). `current` names the step to point at, or is null once there is nothing left; `ready` says expenses are arriving on their own right now, which does not require a Gmail confirmation — somebody forwarding each alert by hand is connected too. `unapproved_senders` names whoever is being turned away by the allow-list, the one failure that looks exactly like silence from a screen; it is empty once `ready`.

Nothing here is stored progress: there is no endpoint to advance a step. The state is derived from the inbox record on every call, so it is the same in every browser and cannot drift from what the mailbox did. Two of the four steps close in a worker — Google confirms a forwarding request by mailing an address only this deployment can read — which is why this is cheap enough to poll while a user watches the screen.

request.description: A local testing seam, not a product path — only mounted when ENVIRONMENT=local. Stands in for the ingest worker: accepts one raw email body directly, bypassing IMAP and the shared ingest mailbox entirely. `recipient` must be a real forwarding address from Get inbox. Always 202, even for an unknown recipient.
Categories, sorts, statuses, alias origins and counterparty kinds. Supersedes Categories, which stays for clients already calling it.

query.description: true adds how many merchants sit in each category — the number a "this will move N comercios" confirmation needs. Costs a read of the caller's merchants, so every dropdown leaves it off

request.description:
Everything the caller may file a merchant under, in dropdown order: the categories the app ships, then the ones they wrote for themselves. Authenticated because half of the answer is theirs, which is also why the catalog above cannot publish it.

custom says which half a value came from. label is English for the shipped ones (value is the stable part; a client showing another language builds its own words from it) and the user's own text for theirs.

usage is null unless with_usage asked for it.

A category of one's own, for spending the shipped list does not describe.

The name is the whole request: the key its merchants are stored under is derived from it (`Mascotas` -> `custom:mascotas`) and is neither chosen by the client nor changeable later. At most 24 characters — it is read in a dropdown, in a chip beside a movement and in a chart legend on a phone.

409 when that name is already taken, accents and case folded away.

Fix the name of a category of one's own — a typo, a better word.

Nothing filed under it moves: the value merchants are stored under is opaque and permanent, and was never the name. The new name shows up everywhere at once, past movements included, because a movement's category is its merchant's and that is joined when an answer is read.

409 when that name is already one of theirs, or when the key names a category the app ships — those are code, the same for everybody.

Remove a category of one's own, and say what moved.

Every merchant filed under it goes back to `uncategorized`, and their movements follow. Nothing else is deleted, and those merchants keep whatever review status they had: removing a bucket is not reviewing what was in it. The response says how many moved.

409 for a category the app ships; 422 for one that is not this caller's.

query.description: Free text, matched against merchant/alias names
One of the Categories values, e.g. groceries or custom:mascotas. One this caller does not have is a 422, not an empty page.
true / false
name | last_seen | times_seen

request.description: Scoped to the authenticated caller only. `needs_review` in the response counts across everything the user owns, not just this page, so a badge does not move while typing in the search box.
Full detail, including every alias (child spelling). 404 both when the id never existed and when it belongs to another user.

Rename, recategorize, or both — at least one of the two fields is required. Either counts as reviewing it, so it leaves the review queue. category is any value GET /merchants/categories lists for this caller — one the app ships, or one they wrote.
Accepts the merchant as it stands, guessed children (aliases) included.
Reattaches one spelling (alias) from the merchant in the path to `target_merchant_id`. Permanent: from here on that spelling resolves by exact match, never re-derived by a rule.
Pulls one spelling out of the merchant in the path into a brand-new merchant of its own, and returns that new merchant. 201 on success.
Folds `absorbed_merchant_id` into the merchant named in the path, which survives with everything the absorbed one had.

item.name: Financial
item.description: Accounts are declared, never discovered. Finflow works with none at all — every alert is recorded and every movement stays unassigned, which is a complete answer for somebody who only wants to see what came in and what went out. Declaring an account is what starts the association, and it is retroactive: the alerts that already arrived under that card are adopted and the balance replays from them.

request.description: Every vocabulary this context's endpoints accept: account kinds (each with the side of net worth it lands on), currencies, movement directions, transaction origins and statuses, account scopes and summary groupings. Call it before rendering any form that posts here. The instrument vocabulary is Ingestion's — see Ingestion > Catalog.

query.description: open | closed | all

request.description: Every account the caller declared, with what each holds now, plus net worth per currency. Balances are signed: an asset legitimately goes below zero when no opening balance was stated, and a liability's positive amount is what is owed.

Declare an account. `instrument_kind` must come from `/financial/catalog` -> instrument_kinds: it is what the BANK calls the thing the money moved through, not what you call the account. A savings account is kind `savings`, and its transfers arrive as instrument `account`. On a liability, `opening_balance` is what has been spent so far and `credit_limit` is what may be spent — two different numbers.
An account belonging to somebody else reads as missing rather than forbidden.
Renaming changes nothing else — balance and instruments stay.

Correct what the account holds, without touching a single movement. Send the figure the bank shows **today** — not the opening balance, which is solved backwards from this and the movements already on record. For declaring an account when nobody remembers what it held before the alerts Finflow already has: open it at zero, then restate. Signed, so an overdrawn account and an overpaid card can both be stated; on a liability the figure is what is owed. Works on a closed account too.

State or restate what this card may owe. Liabilities only. Send null to clear it. The response carries `available` = limit minus what is owed, signed: a card over its limit reports a negative rather than zero.

Teach an account another of the names its alerts arrive under, and adopt retroactively everything already waiting under it. ONE REAL ACCOUNT HAS SEVERAL: a savings account emails as instrument `account` under the account's last four for transfers, and as `debit_card` under the CARD's last four for purchases. Both must be linked or half its movements wait forever. `instrument_kind` comes from /financial/catalog.

Stops this account answering to one card, and lets its movements go. THE FIX FOR A CARD ON THE WRONG ACCOUNT: the movements that arrived under it go back to unassigned, so linking the same card on the right account adopts them. Named by the same three parts Link instrument took, not by the stored key. 409 when this account never answered to it — presumably it is on another one.

Stops taking movements, keeping the history and the balance. Not a delete: a closed account still explains past spending, and a paid-off loan closing at zero is exactly what should stay visible. List it again with ?scope=closed or ?scope=all.

Takes movements again on an account closed by mistake. The history never went anywhere, so nothing is restored: what comes back is only what closing took away — new movements, and being adopted by an alert again. Reopening one that was never closed is not an error.

item.name: Financing
item.description:
Accounts whose balance moves without anybody spending anything: a loan charging interest and insurance every month, a CDT earning at an agreed rate, a fund whose value is stated rather than computed.

**A loan and a mortgage are watched, never counted.** They carry `informational: true` and stay out of net worth, out of what the API reports as owed, and out of every total in `/summary`, `/trends` and `/history` — their owner already knows what they owe, and the cuota that services them is money leaving a real account, already recorded as it leaves. A credit card is not in that bucket: what it owes is this month's spending, unpaid.

The order is: declare the terms once, then post what each closed period charged (`/accrue`, safe to call as often as you like), then read the amortization table and the payoff (`GET .../financing`).

request.description:
What a loan costs, so what is owed can be more than what is unpaid. Loans and mortgages only — a credit card is deliberately excluded, since its interest is charged on whatever part of the statement went unpaid and nothing here knows that.

`rate.value` is a fraction (0.1956, never 19.56) in the basis the bank quotes: `effective_annual` (% E.A.), `nominal_annual` (N.A. M.V.) or `monthly`. Amounts are bare figures in the account's own currency.

`installment_covers_charges` says whether the number on the statement already includes the insurance; getting it backwards misstates the capital portion by exactly the insurance, every month.

`accrue_from` left out means **today**: somebody declaring a mortgage they have paid for three years states the balance their bank shows, and that figure already contains those three years of interest. Send the disbursement date, with the amount disbursed as the opening balance, to rebuild the history instead.

How an investment earns. Investment accounts only.

Leave `rate` out for variable income — shares, a fund whose unit price moves: nothing about those can be computed, and their value is stated through `POST .../value` instead. *Retención en la fuente* is a charge quoted on `earnings`, not on the balance.
Stop computing charges, keeping every period already posted. Those are movements like any other and the balance is their running total, so taking them back would be inventing a different history.

La tabla de amortización, what settling today would take, and — for an investment — what it has actually made.

Every row splits the instalment into interest, charges and the part that reduces the debt, which is the only figure that moves it. `negatively_amortizing` is true when the instalment does not even cover the interest, so the debt grows however long it is paid. `pending_interest` is the days since the last cut that nobody has been charged for yet, and `payoff` is the balance plus that.

Worked out from the balance the ledger holds now, never from the amount originally borrowed. Nothing is stored: the table assumes every instalment is paid on the day it is due.

Turn the closed periods into ledger rows: a month of interest, the insurance it carried, the withholding on what a CDT earned. Each becomes an ordinary movement with `origin: accrual`, so the balance stays the running total of things somebody can read and the credit's own screen can explain itself. Those rows do **not** count as spending: a loan is informational, and the expense is the cuota leaving a real account, which is already recorded there.

Safe to call as often as you like: each charge is identified by its account and its period, so a second call is refused by the ledger's own key and `skipped` says how many.

`through` left out means today, read in `timezone`.

item.name: Post what the month charged (every account)

request.description: The same sweep for every financed account this user holds — the shape a scheduled run wants, and the shape a screen wants when it opens. Accounts with nothing to charge answer with a `reason` rather than an error.

item.name: State what an investment is worth

request.description:
For everything a rate cannot describe: a share price, a fund's unit value.

Not the same thing as `PUT .../balance`. A restatement solves the opening balance backwards, which is right for a savings account whose history is incomplete and wrong here — the gain would live in the opening balance and every report would answer that the position returned nothing. This records the difference **as a movement** instead. Stating the value it already has changes nothing and is not an error.

Assets minus liabilities, one figure per currency held — never summed across them, because that would need an exchange rate nobody recorded. Empty for somebody who declared no accounts, which is an ordinary answer.

Two guesses about the month: what it is supposed to bring in, and how much of that is not to be spent. One currency for both — subtracting a target in dollars from an income in pesos needs a rate this app does not have, and treating the two as comparable is the kind of wrong that looks right. `expected_income` must be greater than zero; `savings_target` is optional, defaults to 0 and is never larger than the income, because a plan that is short before a peso is spent is not a warning anybody can act on. A `PUT` and not a `PATCH` on purpose: a plan is two figures that are both guesses, and replacing it whole is what stops a savings target outliving the income it was set against. **Nothing is recorded as earned or spent** — this writes two numbers and a currency, no ledger row and no balance.

What is declared, plus `updated_at` in epoch seconds — a plan is a guess that gets corrected, so how old it is matters. **404 when nothing is declared**, deliberately: "no plan" is a different thing from "a plan of zero", and only one of them is a state somebody can be in. A zero would read as "you have nothing left to spend".

Take the plan back: 204, and silent when there was nothing to forget — a 404 on the second press of a button somebody is unsure about is a worse answer than nothing. Nothing else changes, because the plan never wrote anything: no movement, no balance, nothing left behind to explain. The allowance goes back to 404 along with it.

query.description: Decides which month 'this month' is.

request.description: What is left to spend this month, and every piece of the subtraction behind it: `available` is `expected_income` less `savings_target`, `spent` and `committed`. The parts are not decoration — a figure nobody can take apart is one they stop believing the first time it disagrees with their own arithmetic. `committed` is what this month's declared bills **still owe**, never what the month costs: a charge already confirmed is counted in `spent`, through the ledger row confirming it wrote, and counting it here too would discount it twice. `available` can be negative and is reported negative rather than floored at zero, because somebody who overspent needs to see by how much. `since` and `until` are the calendar month read in `timezone` and not in UTC — a Bogotá month starting five hours early would count the last evening of the previous one; `days_left` includes today, which is still a day to get through. 404 when no plan is declared, for the reason `GET /financial/plan` gives.

request.description:
What a period adds up to, totalled per currency and never across them. Takes the same filters as `GET /financial/transactions`, so any bucket here opens as a list by repeating the query with the bucket's `key`. A `key` of null is the bucket the grouping could not place — a movement no account claimed, or a counterparty no merchant owns yet — and it belongs in the answer: without it the groups stop adding up to `totals`.

Stretches of time come back newest first and weekdays run Monday to Sunday; every other grouping comes back biggest first, by movement count unless `order=amount` and a `currency` were both asked for.

`others` is what `top` left out, added together. It carries no key on purpose: unlike a real bucket it cannot be reopened as the list behind it. `groups` plus `others` always adds up to `totals`.

request.description:
How spending moved over time, split into the bands a chart stacks.

`/financial/summary` answers one dimension at a time — what a period adds up to, or how it splits by category, never both. This answers the two together: restaurants against transport against groceries, month by month. Asking `/summary` for that a month at a time is twelve round trips whose buckets can each be ranked differently, so they cannot be stacked without reconciling them first.

Two guarantees are what a chart needs. The bands are **ranked once over the whole range**, so every bucket stacks the same ones in the same order. And the buckets are **dense**, with each series holding exactly one point per bucket in the same order: a month nothing happened in is a zero, so zip `series[].points` against `buckets` by index and never fill a gap.

Takes the same filters as `GET /financial/transactions`, so any band opens as the list behind it by repeating the query with the band's `key`. `others` and the unplaced band both carry a null key and cannot be reopened that way.

request.description: Newest first, each movement carrying the canonical `merchant` behind its counterparty text (null while no merchant owns that spelling). `unassigned=true` is the queue somebody works through after declaring an account — or the whole ledger, for somebody who declared none.

Money that moved without an alert to announce it: an automatic payment the bank stays quiet about, cash, a transfer that produced no email.

direction: outgoing | incoming. amount is a string, never a JSON number — a float loses cents. occurred_at is epoch seconds. account_id is optional: somebody watching only what comes in and goes out has no accounts.

category is optional and is about the counterparty, not this one movement: sending it files that name under that category for good, which is what keeps a hand-written movement out of the "no merchant" bucket every breakdown by category leaves out. It applies to past movements with the same counterparty too, because the attribution is joined when an answer is read. Any value GET /merchants/categories lists for this caller; anything else is a 422 and nothing is written.

body.raw:
{
  "role": "destination",
  "amount": "150000",
  "currency": "COP",
  "occurred_at": 1787500000,
  "counterparty": "Nequi",
  "account_id": "{{account_id}}",
  "bank": "Bancolombia",
  "note": "pago de la tarjeta desde otro banco"
}

request.description:
A payment between two of the owner's own balances whose other side this app does not hold: a credit card paid from another bank, from a wallet, or in cash.

Paying a card from an account at the SAME bank needs nothing here — that alert names both instruments and the two linked rows are written from it. This is the other case, where no single alert can name both, and recording it as an ordinary movement would count the payment as income on the card or as an expense on the account it left.

role: source (money left the named account) | destination (it arrived; on a credit card that is its debt going down). There is no `direction` — role fixes it.

account_id is REQUIRED, unlike the plain manual entry: this asserts that a balance moved, and a leg names no instrument, so nothing could ever adopt it later. counterparty is free text for whatever the owner calls the other side ("Nequi", "efectivo", "PSE"). amount is a string, never a JSON number.

The answer carries transfer.external = true and every transfer.counterpart_* field null. The movement is listed by GET /financial/transactions and left out of /summary, /trends and /history — which is the whole point of entering it this way.

IDEMPOTENT: the movement id is derived from user + account + role + amount + occurred_at + counterparty, and the ledger write is conditional on it. Sending this request twice answers 201 twice with the SAME movement and moves the balance once — send it again to see it. `bank` and `note` are not part of that identity; changing the amount, the instant, the role or the counterparty makes it a different payment.
`stated` is present only once somebody corrected this movement, and holds what the bank originally said.

Everything omitted is left alone; at least one field is required. Changing the amount needs its currency too.

On a movement that came from a bank alert, the first correction keeps what the bank said in `stated` — that is how a balance that looks wrong can be traced back to whether the alert or the correction was the mistake. The identity never moves with an edit, so a redelivery of a corrected alert still lands on the same row.

account_id moves it to another account; detach takes it off whatever holds it. Not both. Either way the affected balances replay from the ledger.

Erases the movement and gives the balance back what it took: a 2000 purchase deleted is 2000 the account holds again. The balance is recomputed from the rows that remain rather than nudged by the amount, so it cannot end up disagreeing with them.

Not the same as PATCH with detach, which only takes the movement off its account — that one still exists and still counts in what came in and went out.

Both sides of a transfer go together: erasing either row of a payment between two of the owner's own accounts erases the other and restores both balances. A leg paid from outside this app has no second row and goes alone.

Answers `erased` (every movement id that left) and `accounts` (the accounts whose balances changed, already recomputed — empty when the movement was on no account). 404 for a movement that is not there, including a second delete of one already erased.

query.description: ISO date. Both ends or neither.
ISO date. At most 400 days from `since`.
Decides which month 'this month' is.

request.description: Declared bills, every charge falling inside the window, and what it adds up to. The window defaults to the calendar month `timezone` is currently in; give both ends or neither. Two totals per currency and never one: `expected` is what the window costs, `outstanding` what nobody has answered for yet — it was called `upcoming` and meant "has not fallen due", which was all it could mean before charges could be confirmed. A paid charge stays in `expected` and leaves `outstanding`; a skipped one leaves both. Each occurrence carries its `state` (`expected`, `overdue`, `paid`, `skipped`) and, once paid, the `movement_id` behind it with what actually moved. `frozen` means the bill's account is closed; it is derived from the account, so reopening it un-freezes the bill.

A charge the owner says is going to happen, every so often — the gym, the rent, a domiciled subscription the bank stopped emailing about. **Nothing is recorded as spent:** a bill is a statement about the future, and it reaches the ledger only when a charge is confirmed. `starts_on` is the first expected charge and the day every later one derives from, which is why a bill anchored on the 31st lands on the 28th in February and is back on the 31st in March.

Correct what the bill says: the gym raised its price, the charge moved to another account, the day turned out to be the 6th. What is absent is left alone — so taking the account or the category off needs `clear_account` / `clear_category`, since absence already means 'leave it'. Changing the amount needs its currency too.
Stop expecting charges without forgetting what it cost. The cancelled subscription. A paused bill predicts nothing and adds nothing to any total.
Expect charges again, from the same anchor day.

Say one charge of one period happened, and write it into the ledger. **The only call under `/bills` that moves money**, and it goes through the same use case as `POST /financial/transactions`, so the balance, the merchant attribution, the month's spending and the Telegram alert all follow. The period in the path is the charge's `due_on` and has to be a day the bill is actually charged on — without it, "paid" in September and in October would be the same request. Calling it twice is one charge and answers 200 both times: the row's id comes from the bill and the period, so the second write is refused by DynamoDB rather than by a check. An empty body `{}` confirms what the bill says, on the period's own day at noon UTC; send `amount` (with its `currency`) when the price changed, and `occurred_at` (epoch seconds) when the money moved on another day. Neither takes part in the identity, so correcting a figure by calling again cannot write a second row — edit the movement instead. 409 when the bill's account is closed.

Erase the movement the confirmation wrote. The account gets back exactly what the charge took, because that is what erasing a movement already does — and "paid" is never stored anywhere, it is read back off that very row, so removing the row is the whole of removing the answer. Silent (200) when there is nothing to erase: this is the undo behind a button somebody presses because they are unsure.

Say this charge is not going to happen — the month the gym did not bill, the subscription cancelled before its renewal. Writes nothing to the ledger and takes the charge out of **both** of the month's figures. Unlike "paid", this one *is* stored on the bill: no money moves, so there is no row to read the answer back off. 400 on a charge that is already paid — undo the payment first, or the figures would stop adding up with nothing on screen saying why.

Let a skipped charge be expected again. No calendar check, on purpose: amending the bill's day can leave a skip on a date the calendar no longer visits, and refusing to remove that would make it permanent.

A real delete, unlike closing an account: a closed account still explains movements in the ledger, and a bill explains nothing because it never wrote anything. Pausing is for the one worth keeping. 204, or 404 when there was nothing there.

query.description: IANA name. Decides which day each charge fell on: nine at night in Bogotá is the 15th there and the 16th in UTC, and a series whose days alternate between the two has no cadence left to find.

request.description:
The detector half of bills: what looks like it comes back every so often and is nobody's declared bill yet, read off thirteen months of movements. A proposal and nothing more — this writes nothing, and accepting one is `POST /financial/bills` with these figures, the same call anybody declares a bill with, so whatever ends up able to charge money is always something a person stated.

The window (`since`, `until`, `months`) comes back so a screen can say what "nothing found" was looked for in: an empty list is the ordinary answer for somebody two weeks in, and it means "not enough history yet", not "you have no subscriptions".

Left out on purpose: charges this app wrote itself — the interest a credit accrues every cut is perfectly monthly and would head the ranking, and a confirmed bill charge would be the detector reading its own handwriting — and transfers, because paying the card from savings every month is the most regular charge anybody has and it is not a subscription. Dormant series (two expected charges missed) are dropped rather than proposed; a list that suggests declaring a cancelled subscription is one nobody reads twice.

`bill_id` is the mark that matters: non-null means this series is already declared, and the screen should not offer it again. `amount` is what the *next* charge is expected to cost, a median when `variable` is true, so "about $90.000" and "$90.000" stay different promises. Ordered by `confidence` (0 to 1) — it ranks a list read top-down and decides nothing, which is why there is no threshold anywhere in this feature. At most 40 series, a bound rather than a page.

request.description:
Opens a channel and returns the deep link that binds it. Following that link in Telegram and pressing Start is what verifies it — there is no code to type and no chat id to look up.

`link_url` is returned **once**. It is not stored (only its hash is) and `GET /alerts/channels` cannot hand it back, so losing it means asking for another. Asking again also retires whatever attempt was outstanding, so one account never has two live links at a time.

201 on success; 409 when the account already holds as many channels as it may.

Every channel this caller owns, bound or still waiting. The screen polls this while a link is outstanding: binding happens inside Telegram, where the page cannot see it.

Never carries the link, and never the full chat id — `chat_hint` is its last few characters, which is all the owner needs to recognise which account is bound. Every alert type appears in `preferences`, including ones nobody has expressed an opinion about yet, so a screen can draw a switch for each without guessing the default.

Says how much of one kind of alert this channel wants.

`minimum_amount` is a string, like money everywhere else here, and `null` clears the floor. Below the floor nothing is sent — it is about noise, not about money: a three-thousand-peso coffee should not spend the attention a four-hundred-thousand-peso charge needs. A floor in one currency never silences a movement in another.

404 for a channel that is not yours, which is the same answer a malformed id gets.
Unlinks a destination. Nothing more is sent to it, and the Telegram account it held is free to be bound again — by anyone. 204 on success, 404 for a channel that is not yours.

What Telegram posts when somebody presses Start. **This is a product path, not a local seam** — unlike `/ingestion/bank-notifications`, it is mounted in every environment and is how every channel gets bound. It sits under Local testing only because a laptop is the one place you have to play Telegram yourself; `just telegram-update <token>` does the same thing from a terminal.

Authenticated by the shared secret header alone, compared in constant time, and checked before the body is parsed. A wrong or missing header is 403; **everything else answers 200**, including an unknown, spent or expired token — Telegram retries any non-2xx and eventually disables the webhook, and answering alike keeps the endpoint from saying whether a link exists. Check `GET /alerts/channels` to see whether the channel actually bound.
